newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong dollar seen unchanged by handover.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong dollar seen unchanged by handover.

text.p: Rock solid under pressure, Hong Kong's fixed currency first rescued the territory from financial chaos in 1983 when Sino-British negotiations over the terms of Hong Kong's return to China roiled markets.

The link has stood firm ever since, anchoring the territory's open economy through many storms, including a speculative attack in January 1995, a stock market plunge following the Tiananmen massacre in 1989 and the global stock market crash of 1987.

On Monday, one week before the handover event that prompted the creation of the fixed exchange rate, experts took the opportunity to reassure everybody, once again, that no change is likely when China takes charge at midnight on June 30.

"It's easy to put a political spin on this but overall Hong Kong's importance to China is economic," T.C. Chan, head of commercial banking for Citibank in Hong Kong, told a conference organised by the Far Eastern Economic Review.
"China clearly sees that and there is absolutely no economic reason for them to tamper with the current system," he said.
Hong Kong's dollar, fixed at a rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar, has provided 14 years of stability for foreign investors, Hong Kong business and local people.

Armed with US$63 billion in foreign exchange reserves and a fistful of agreements with other Asian nations -- including China, which has US$115 billion in reserves -- Hong Kong is well defended against any speculative assault.

Hong Kong's foreign exchange reserves amount to 32 percent of the entire Hong Kong dollar M2 float, suggesting that the currency would be well defended even against massive capital flight sparked by external shock, Chan said.

The integrity of the Hong Kong dollar link underscores the commitments made by China to Hong Kong's role as an autonomous fiscal and monetary region, said Norman Chan, deputy chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's de facto central bank.

Handover agreements and constant commitments from Chinese leaders, central bankers and Hong Kong's post-handover chief executive Tung Chee-hwa have guaranteed that the existing system would continue unchanged for many years, the HKMA's Chan said.

He and other experts dismissed any prospect of change to the existing system, arguing that allowing the currency to float freely or switching the link from the U.S. dollar to a basket of currencies would compromise the financial and monetary stability Hong Kong has worked so hard to establish.

"The commitments to a separate and autonomous fiscal and monetary system for Hong Kong after the transition are clear and unequivocal and are enshrined in the Basic Law, Hong Kong's post-1997 constitution," Richard Margolis, political analyst with Merrill Lynch, said recently.

"The evidence of the manner in which these issues were handled during the negotiations on Hong Kong's future is that China regards the peg as an integral part of a winning recipe that operates to China's advantage as well as Hong Kong's."
Virtually no currency movement has been detected in the months leading up to the handover.
Although currency forwards widened a few weeks ago in anticipation of potential instability surrounding the handover, the market has returned to normal with one week to go.
The Hong Kong dollar is trading at HK$7.7440 with little activity in interest rates or currency forwards.
